name: Luna 25
short_status: Crashed into the Moon 19 Aug 2023 after an orbit-lowering burn ran 43 seconds long; NASA's LRO photographed the ~10 m crater on 24 Aug 2023.
tagline: Roscosmos · Russia · Lander · 2023 · Commercial and multipolar Failure
stats: since Russia's previous lunar mission, Luna 24 in 1976

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 10 Aug 2023, 23:10 UTC, on a Soyuz-2.1b with Fregat upper stage from Vostochny Cosmodrome; first Russian lunar mission since Luna 24 in 1976

facts.label: Spacecraft
facts.value: 1,750 kg launch mass, built by NPO Lavochkin, carrying about 30 kg of science payload (8 instruments including ADRON-LR neutron/gamma spectrometer, LASMA-LR laser mass spectrometer, STS-L cameras, plus a robotic sampling arm)

facts.label: Planned landing
facts.value: 21 Aug 2023, north of Boguslawsky crater at about 69.545 S, 43.544 E; a high-southern-latitude site well short of the south pole itself

facts.label: Failure
facts.value: 19 Aug 2023: pre-landing orbit-lowering burn ran 127 seconds instead of the planned 84 (per Roscosmos chief Yuri Borisov); contact lost the same day, impact at 11:58 UTC; Roscosmos declared the spacecraft lost on 20 Aug 2023

facts.label: Investigation finding
facts.value: 3 Oct 2023: Roscosmos attributed the crash to abnormal operation of the onboard control system after the accelerometer unit in the BIUS-L angular-velocity device failed to switch on, likely because commands with different priorities entered one data array; with zero accelerometer signals the engine could not be cut off at the target velocity and shut down only on a backup timer

facts.label: Crash site found
facts.value: LRO imaged a new crater about 10 m across on 24 Aug 2023 at 57.865 S, 61.360 E (elevation about minus 360 m) on the southwest rim of Pontecoulant G, roughly 400 km short of the intended landing site; NASA announced it 31 Aug 2023 as "likely" from Luna 25 because the crater was absent in June 2022 imagery and matched Russia's published impact estimate

facts.label: Luna 26 status
facts.value: Orbiter delayed to targeted 2028 launch (as of Aug 2025 RAS statements, reaffirmed by RAS vice president Sergei Chernyshev on 7 Apr 2026 and by NPO Lavochkin's Feb 2026 presentation); it slipped after the Luna 25 failure, with contractor NPO Lavochkin receiving added funding

facts.label: Luna 27 status
facts.value: Doubled into two landers (as of 4 Feb 2026, per NPO Lavochkin director general Vasily Marfin): Luna-27A targeted 2029 to the south polar region and Luna-27B targeted 2030 to the north polar region

facts.label: Later Luna missions
facts.value: Still slipping: on 7 Apr 2026 RAS vice president Sergei Chernyshev gave Luna-29 in 2032, Luna-30 in 2034 and sample-return Luna-28 in 2036, contradicting NPO Lavochkin's February 2026 figure of 2034 for Luna-28

timeline: Launch at 23:10 UTC on Soyuz-2.1b/Fregat from Vostochny Cosmodrome
Orbit-lowering burn runs 127 s instead of 84 s; contact lost; impact at 11:58 UTC on the rim of Pontecoulant G
Planned landing date near Boguslawsky crater (never attempted)
LRO images a fresh ~10 m crater at the predicted impact point; NASA announces the find 31 Aug
Roscosmos names the probable cause: failure of the BIUS-L accelerometer unit left the control system with zero velocity signals during the burn
RAS confirms follow-on Luna 26 orbiter delayed to targeted 2028
NPO Lavochkin outlines two Luna 27 landers: 27A targeted 2029 (south polar), 27B targeted 2030 (north polar)
